dhpak1.9:1.1: 1.8 The Story about the Chief Disciples Aggasāvakavatthu
dhpak1.9:2.1: “Finding the essential in the unessential,” this {1.83} Dhamma teaching was given by the Teacher while he was in residence
dhpak1.9:2.2: at Veḷuvana in Rājagaha, and it was with reference to the announcement made by the Chief Disciples of Sañjaya’s refusal
dhpak1.9:2.3: to go to the Teacher. From first to last the story is as follows:
dhpak1.9:4.1: Four immeasurables and 100,000 aeons of time in the past our Teacher was born as a Brahmin prince in the city of Amaravatī,
dhpak1.9:4.2: and his name was Sumedha. After acquiring proficiency in all the arts, he renounced wealth amounting to countless millions
dhpak1.9:4.3: which he inherited on the death of his mother and father, went forth, went forth amongst the seers, took up his residence
dhpak1.9:4.4: in the Himālaya country, and there won for himself the absorptions and the super knowledges.
dhpak1.9:5.1: Now it came to pass on a certain day that [28.194] Dīpaṅkara, the One of Ten Strengths, set out from Sudassana monastery
dhpak1.9:5.2: to go to the city of Ramma, and the populace came forth to clear the way. As Sumedha came flying through the air on that day,
dhpak1.9:5.3: he observed that a road was being cleared. Therefore selecting for himself a portion of the road which had not yet been cleared,
dhpak1.9:5.4: when the Teacher approached, he made of himself a bridge for him, spread his mantle of antelope skin in the mud,
dhpak1.9:5.5: laid himself thereon, and said: “Let not the Teacher with his company of disciples tread upon the mud. Let him rather tread upon me;
dhpak1.9:5.6: so let him proceed upon his journey.”
dhpak1.9:6.1: When the Teacher beheld Sumedha, he said: “Yonder prince is a nascent Buddha; four immeasurables and 100,000 aeons of time
dhpak1.9:6.2: hence {1.84} he will become a Buddha named Gotama.” After Dīpaṅkara came the following Buddhas: Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, Sumana,
dhpak1.9:6.3: Revata, Sobhita, Anomadassī, Paduma, Nārada, Padumuttara, Sumedha, Sujāta, Piyadassī, Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, Siddhattha,
dhpak1.9:6.4: Tissa, Phussa, Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa. One after another these twenty-four Buddhas
dhpak1.9:6.5: arose in the world and enlightened the world, and from each of them the Brahmin prince Sumedha received the prophecy.
dhpak1.9:7.1: Now after Sumedha had fulfilled the ten perfections and the ten minor perfections and the ten major perfections,
dhpak1.9:7.2: making in all thirty perfections, he was reborn as Vessantara; and in his existence as Vessantara he bestowed mighty alms
dhpak1.9:7.3: which caused the earth to quake, and in that existence also he renounced both son and wife. When the term of life allotted
dhpak1.9:7.4: to him was come to an end, he was reborn in the Tusita Realm; and when he had remained in this state of existence during
dhpak1.9:7.5: the term of life allotted to him, the Devatās of the 10,000 world-system assembled together and thus addressed him:
dhpak1.9:8.1: It is time, Deva, Great Hero, to arise in your mother’s womb, crossing the world with its Devas, awaken to the Deathless State.
dhpak1.9:9.1: Thereupon he made the five great observations, and passing from that state of existence, received a new existence in the
dhpak1.9:10.1: In this royal household he was brought up amid great splendor and in the course of time attained auspicious youth.
dhpak1.9:10.2: He spent his youth in three mansions appropriate to the three seasons of the year, enjoying splendor and majesty of
dhpak1.9:10.3: sovereignty comparable [28.195] to the splendor of the Deva Realm. In the course of time it came to pass that,
dhpak1.9:10.4: as he proceeded on three successive days to the garden to amuse himself, he beheld the three heavenly messengers;
dhpak1.9:10.5: namely, a man worn out by old age, a man afflicted with disease, and a dead man. {1.85} On each of the three days he
dhpak1.9:10.6: returned to his palace, overcome with emotion.
dhpak1.9:11.1: On the fourth day he beheld a man who had gone forth. “It were well for me to go forth,” said he, conceiving a desire for the going forth;
dhpak1.9:11.2: and with this thought in mind, he proceeded to the garden and spent the entire day sitting on the bank of the royal pool.
dhpak1.9:11.3: While he sat there, the god Vissakamma approached him, disguised as a barber, and dressed him in rich apparel and adorned
dhpak1.9:11.4: him with all manner of adornments. There also he received the message that a son had been born to him, Prince Rāhula;
dhpak1.9:11.5: and realizing the strength of affection for a son, he reflected: “I must straightaway break this bond, lest it become too strong for me.”
dhpak1.9:11.6: In the evening, as he entered the city, Kisā Gotamī, daughter of his father’s sister, pronounced the following verse:
dhpak1.9:12.1: Happy indeed is that mother, happy indeed is that father, happy indeed is that wife whose husband is such a one as this.
dhpak1.9:13.1: When he heard Kisā Gotamī pronounce this verse, he said: “This woman has taught me where true happiness is to be found,”
dhpak1.9:13.2: and taking off a string of pearls, he sent it to her as a present. Having entered his own residence, he lay down on the royal couch,
dhpak1.9:13.3: and as he lay there beheld the disgusting appearance of the dancing girls asleep.
dhpak1.9:14.1: Heartsick he roused his courtier Channa, caused his steed Kanthaka to be brought to him, mounted Kanthaka,
dhpak1.9:14.2: and taking Channa with him as his companion, and surrounded by the Devatās of the 10,000 world-system, he went forth and
dhpak1.9:14.3: made the Great Renunciation. Proceeding to the bank of the river Anoma, he went forth, proceeded to Rājagaha and went
dhpak1.9:15.1: Then he went forth to Mount Paṇḍava and seated himself in Paṇḍava mountain cave. While he was sitting there,
dhpak1.9:15.2: the king of Magadha came to him and offered to bestow his kingdom upon him, but this offer of the king he straightaway refused.
dhpak1.9:15.3: He promised the king, however, to visit his kingdom so soon as he should attain omniscience. Then he approached [28.196] Āḷāra and Uddaka;
dhpak1.9:15.4: but after following their system of discipline, failed to win the attainment which distinguishes one who has attained Arahatship.
dhpak1.9:15.5: Thereafter, for a period of six years, he engaged in the great striving.
dhpak1.9:16.1: Early in the morning on the day of the full moon of the month Visākhā {1.86} he ate rice-porridge presented to him by Sujātā,
dhpak1.9:16.2: caused his golden bowl to float on the river Nerañjarā, and spent the day in Mahāvana Grove in the various degrees of absorption.
dhpak1.9:16.3: In the evening he listened to the praise of his noble qualities bestowed upon him by the Nāga king Kāḷa, ascended the throne of wisdom,
dhpak1.9:16.4: received the bundles of grass presented to him by Sotthiya, scattered the grass before him, and formed the following resolution:
dhpak1.9:16.5: “I will not abandon this posture until I have utterly ceased to care for the things of this world and my heart has rid
dhpak1.9:17.1: Thereupon he sat down facing the east, and before the sun had set overcame the host of Māra. In the first watch he acquired
dhpak1.9:17.2: the knowledge of previous states of existence; in the second watch he acquired the knowledge of the vanishing of creatures
dhpak1.9:17.3: from one state of existence and of their reappearance in another; at the conclusion of the last watch he acquired the
dhpak1.9:17.4: knowledge of the causes of existence, fathoming the depths of omniscience and acquiring the Ten Strengths,
dhpak1.9:17.5: the four subjects of confidence, and all of the noble qualities.
dhpak1.9:18.1: For seven weeks he remained on the throne of wisdom; in the eighth week he seated himself under the Goatherd’s Banyan tree
dhpak1.9:18.2: and meditated upon the depths of the Dhamma, finally arriving at misgivings as to his ability to teach the Dhamma to others.
dhpak1.9:19.1: Straightaway Sahampati Brahma, accompanied by the retinue of the 10,000 world-system with which Mahā Brahma is wont to be accompanied,
dhpak1.9:19.2: approached him and requested him to teach the Dhamma to others. Surveying the world with the eye of a Buddha,
dhpak1.9:19.3: he acceded to Brahma’s request. “To whom, pray, shall I first teach the Dhamma?” thought he. Surveying the world,
dhpak1.9:19.4: he became aware of the death of Āḷāra and Uddaka. But remembering the devoted services of the group of five bhikkhus,
dhpak1.9:19.5: he arose from his seat {1.87} and went to Kāsipura, meeting Upaka by the way and talking with him.
dhpak1.9:20.1: On the day of the full moon of the month Āsāḷha he arrived at Isipatana in the Deer Park, at the place of residence of
dhpak1.9:20.2: the group of five bhikkhus; and when the group of five bhikkhus addressed him improperly, he instructed them how to address him properly.
dhpak1.9:20.3: Then he set in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma, giving to drink of the deathless to 180 millions of [28.197] Brahmas,
dhpak1.9:20.4: with Aññā Koṇḍañña at their head.
dhpak1.9:21.1: Having set in motion the glorious Wheel of the Dhamma, on the fifth day of the half-month he established all those bhikkhus in Arahatship.
dhpak1.9:21.2: On the same day also he perceived that the noble youth Yasa possessed the supporting conditions; and when the noble youth
dhpak1.9:21.3: Yasa left his house in disgust at what he saw during the night, he saw him and summoned him, saying: “Come, Yasa!”
dhpak1.9:21.4: In that same night also he caused him to attain Stream-entry, and on the following day caused him to attain Arahatship.
dhpak1.9:21.5: Afterwards he gave the going forth to his fifty-four companions, employing the formula: “Come, bhikkhus!”
dhpak1.9:21.6: And having made them go forth of them, he caused them to attain Arahatship.
dhpak1.9:22.1: There were thus sixty-one Arahats in the world. Having kept residence during the season of the Rains, and having celebrated
dhpak1.9:22.2: the Invitation, he sent out the sixty bhikkhus into all the world, saying: “Go forth, bhikkhus, and wander.”
dhpak1.9:23.1: He himself proceeded to Uruvelā, on the way there, in Kappāsika grove, instructing the Thirty Youths known as the Fortunate Group.
dhpak1.9:23.2: Of these the least attained Stream-entry and the greatest attained the fruition of Non-returner. All these youths he made
dhpak1.9:23.3: go forth with the single formula: “Come, bhikkhus!” And when he had so done, he sent them all out into the world.
dhpak1.9:24.1: Arriving at Uruvelā, he performed 3,500 miracles {1.88} and converted Uruvelā Kassapa, Nadī Kassapa, and Gayā Kassapa.
dhpak1.9:24.2: These were three brothers, ascetics who wore matted hair, with a following of a thousand disciples.
dhpak1.9:24.3: These ascetics he instructed in the Dhamma. And when he had so done, he let them go forth with the single formula:
dhpak1.9:24.4: “Come, bhikkhus!” Seating them at Gayāsīsa, he established them in Arahatship by teaching the Fire Sermon;
dhpak1.9:24.5: then, attended by a thousand Arahats, he went to Latthivana Garden near the city of Rājagaha, intending to redeem the
dhpak1.9:24.6: promise he had given to King Bimbisāra.
dhpak1.9:25.1: “The Teacher has arrived,” went forth the cry. Hearing the report, King Bimbisāra approached with 120,000 Brahmin householders,
dhpak1.9:25.2: and to him the Buddha taught the Dhamma in a pleasing manner, establishing the king and 110,000 of Brahmins in the fruition
dhpak1.9:25.3: of Stream-entry and 10,000 of Brahmins in the refuges.
dhpak1.9:26.1: On the following day he listened to the praise of his noble qualities by Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, disguised as a Brahmin youth,
dhpak1.9:26.2: and then entered the city of Rājagaha. Having eaten his meal in the royal [28.198] residence, he accepted the gift of
dhpak1.9:26.3: Veḷuvana monastery and took up his residence there. And there it was that Sāriputta and Moggallāna came to him.
dhpak1.9:27.1: 8b The Life of Upatissa (Sāriputta) and Kolita (Moggallāna)
dhpak1.9:28.1: Before the Buddha appeared in the world, there were two Brahmin villages not far from Rājagaha named Upatissa village and Kolita village.
dhpak1.9:28.2: One day a Brahmin’s wife named Rūpasārī, who lived in Upatissa village, conceived a child in her womb;
dhpak1.9:28.3: and on the same day a Brahmin’s wife named Moggalī, who lived in Kolita village, likewise conceived a child in her womb.
dhpak1.9:28.4: We are told that for seven generations these two families had been firmly knit and bound together in the bonds of friendship;
dhpak1.9:28.5: they performed the protection of the womb for the two expectant mothers on the same day. On the expiration of ten lunar months,
dhpak1.9:28.6: both women gave birth to sons.
dhpak1.9:29.1: On the day appointed for the naming of the children, they gave the name Upatissa to the son of the Brahmin woman whose name was Sārī,
dhpak1.9:29.2: because he was the son of the principal family in Upatissa village; {1.89} to the other boy, because he was the son of
dhpak1.9:29.3: the principal family in Kolita village, they gave the name Kolita. As they grew up, both boys attained the highest
dhpak1.9:29.4: proficiency in all the arts and sciences. Whenever the youth Upatissa went to the river or the garden to disport himself,
dhpak1.9:29.5: five hundred golden litters accompanied him; five hundred chariots drawn by thoroughbreds accompanied the youth Kolita.
dhpak1.9:29.6: The two youths had retinues of five hundred Brahmin youths apiece.
dhpak1.9:30.1: Now there is a festival celebrated every year in Rājagaha which goes by the name of the Mountain-Top festival.
dhpak1.9:30.2: A couch for the two youths was set up in one place, and the two youths sat together and witnessed the passing show.
dhpak1.9:30.3: When there was occasion to laugh, they laughed; when there was occasion to weep, they wept; when it was time to give alms,
dhpak1.9:30.4: they gave alms. In this way they witnessed the festivities for several days. But one day, when they had grown wiser,
dhpak1.9:30.5: there was no laughter when they might have laughed, as on preceding days, there were no tears when they might have wept,
dhpak1.9:30.6: and when their alms were sought they gave no alms.
dhpak1.9:31.1: The following thought, we are told, occurred to the two youths: “Why should we look at this? Before a hundred years have passed,
dhpak1.9:31.2: all these people will have gone hence and will no more be seen. It is necessary for us rather to seek the way of release.”
dhpak1.9:31.3: And taking this [28.199] thought to heart, they sat down. Then Kolita said to Upatissa: “Friend Upatissa,
dhpak1.9:31.4: you do not appear to be pleased and delighted as on previous days. Nay rather, you are afflicted with melancholy.
dhpak1.9:31.5: What is in your mind?” – “Friend Kolita, I sit thinking: ‘There is no lasting satisfaction in looking upon these folk;
dhpak1.9:31.6: {1.90} this is all unprofitable; it is necessary for me rather to seek the way of release for myself. But why are you melancholy?”
dhpak1.9:31.7: Kolita said the same thing. When Upatissa discovered that Kolita’s thoughts were one with his own, he said:
dhpak1.9:31.8: “Both of us have had a happy thought. It is necessary for us both to seek the way of release and to go forth together.
dhpak1.9:31.9: Under what teacher shall we go forth?”
dhpak1.9:32.1: Now at this time a wanderer named Sañjaya entered the city of Rājagaha, accompanied by a large retinue of wanderers.
dhpak1.9:32.2: “We will go forth under Sañjaya,” said Upatissa and Kolita. So they dismissed 500 Brahmin youths, saying to them:
dhpak1.9:32.3: “Take the litters and the chariots and go,” and together with the remaining 500, they went forth under Sañjaya.
dhpak1.9:32.4: From the day when these two youths went forth under Sañjaya, Sañjaya reached the pinnacle of gain and renown.
dhpak1.9:32.5: In but a few days they had passed the bounds of Sañjaya’s teaching. Therefore they asked him: “Teacher, is this all the
dhpak1.9:32.6: Dhamma you know, or is there something more besides?” – “This is all there is; you know all.”
dhpak1.9:33.1: Upatissa and Kolita thought to themselves: “If this is the case, it is profitless for us to remain pupils of this teacher any longer.
dhpak1.9:33.2: The way of release we went forth to seek for, we certainly cannot obtain from this teacher. But Jambudīpa is an extensive country.
dhpak1.9:33.3: Let us journey through villages, market-towns, and royal cities. We shall surely find some teacher who will expound to us
dhpak1.9:34.1: From that time forth, wherever they heard there was a learned ascetic or Brahmin, they went to him and held converse with him.
dhpak1.9:34.2: The questions Upatissa and Kolita asked, the others {1.91} were not able to answer; but every question the others asked,
dhpak1.9:34.3: Upatissa and Kolita answered. In this manner they traveled all over Jambudīpa; then they retraced their steps and returned
dhpak1.9:34.4: to their own homes again. Before they separated, Upatissa said to Kolita: “Friend Kolita, whichever of us first attains
dhpak1.9:34.5: the Deathless is to inform the other.” Having made this agreement, they separated.
dhpak1.9:35.1: While they were living under this agreement, the Teacher, after [28.200] traveling from place to place as has been related above,
dhpak1.9:35.2: arrived at Rājagaha, accepted the gift of Veḷuvana monastery, and took up his residence at Veḷuvana.
dhpak1.9:35.3: Now after the Teacher had sent forth the sixty Arahats to proclaim the virtues of the Three Jewels, saying: “Go forth,
dhpak1.9:35.4: bhikkhus, wander for the good of the many,” one of the group of five, the great Elder Assaji, turned back, came to Rājagaha,
dhpak1.9:35.5: and on the following day, early in the morning, taking his bowl and his robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. On the same day,
dhpak1.9:35.6: early in the morning, the wanderer Upatissa ate his breakfast, and proceeding to the hermitage of the wanderers, saw the elder.
dhpak1.9:35.7: When he saw him, he thought to himself: “Never before have I seen one gone forth like this. He must be one of those who
dhpak1.9:35.8: have attained Arahatship in this world, or who have entered upon the path leading to Arahatship. Suppose I were to approach
dhpak1.9:35.9: this bhikkhu and ask him: ‘For whose sake, friend, have you gone forth? And who is your teacher? And whose doctrine do you profess?’”
dhpak1.9:35.10: Then this thought occurred to him: “It is not the proper time to ask this bhikkhu questions, for he is going from house to house for alms.
dhpak1.9:35.11: Suppose I were to follow close in the footsteps of this bhikkhu, as those are wont to do who seek some favor?”
dhpak1.9:36.1: Therefore, observing that the elder had received a portion of alms and was on his way to a certain place, and perceiving
dhpak1.9:36.2: that he desired to sit down, {1.92} he placed his own wanderer’s stool on the ground and offered it to him;
dhpak1.9:36.3: and when he had finished his meal, offered him water from his own waterpot. Having thus performed the duties of a pupil to a teacher,
dhpak1.9:36.4: he exchanged pleasant greetings with the elder after the meal was over and said to him: “Calm and serene, brother,
dhpak1.9:36.5: are your sense organs; clean and clear is the hue of your skin. For whose sake, friend, did you go forth? And who is your teacher?
dhpak1.9:36.6: And whose doctrine do you profess?”
dhpak1.9:37.1: The elder thought: “These wanderers are hostile to the religion I profess; therefore I will show this bhikkhu the profundity of our religion.”
dhpak1.9:37.2: But first he explained that he was himself newly ordained, saying: “Friend, no long time have I gone forth;
dhpak1.9:37.3: but recently did I approach this Doctrine and Discipline; just now I shall not be able to expound the Dhamma at length.”
dhpak1.9:37.4: Thought the wanderer: “I am Upatissa; say much or little according to your ability; I will undertake to fathom the meaning
dhpak1.9:37.5: in a hundred ways or a thousand ways.” Therefore he said:
dhpak1.9:38.1: Speak a little or else speak much, but tell me the substance only, I have need only of the substance, why should you utter many words?
dhpak1.9:39.1: In response the elder pronounced the first line of the verse:
dhpak1.9:40.1: Whatever things have cause and source, their cause the Realised One told.
dhpak1.9:41.1: So soon as the wanderer heard the first line, he was established in Stream-entry, perfect in a thousand ways.
dhpak1.9:41.2: {1.93} So soon as he was established in Stream-entry, the elder completed the second line:
dhpak1.9:42.1: That which is their cessation, such is the Great Ascetic’s doctrine.
dhpak1.9:43.1: Cause and Source But after he had attained Stream-entry, the higher excellence failed to appear. Therefore he considered:
dhpak1.9:43.2: “There must be a reason for this,” and he said to the elder: “Do not carry your teaching of the Dhamma any further;
dhpak1.9:43.3: let this suffice. Where does our Teacher reside?” – “At Veḷuvana, brother.” – “Well then, venerable Sir, you go on ahead.
dhpak1.9:43.4: I have a friend, and he and I made the following agreement with each other: ‘Whichever of us first attains the Deathless
dhpak1.9:43.5: is to inform the other.’ I wish first to redeem this promise. I will bring my friend with me and go to the Teacher,
dhpak1.9:43.6: following the same path you take.” So saying, Upatissa prostrated himself before the feet of the elder with the five limbs,
dhpak1.9:43.7: walked thrice around him clockwise, and then took leave of him and went to meet the leader of the wanderers.
dhpak1.9:44.1: The wanderer Kolita saw him approaching from afar and said to himself: “To-day my friend’s face has a hue not as on other days;
dhpak1.9:44.2: it must be that he has attained the Deathless.” Therefore he asked him at once whether he had attained the Deathless.
dhpak1.9:44.3: Upatissa said in reply: “Yes, brother, I have attained the Deathless.” So saying, he pronounced the same verse Assaji had pronounced.
dhpak1.9:44.4: At the conclusion of the verse Kolita was established in the fruition of Stream-entry. Thereupon Kolita said: “Friend,
dhpak1.9:44.5: where does our Teacher reside?” – “At Veḷuvana, friend. So I was informed by our teacher the Elder Assaji.” – “Well then,
dhpak1.9:44.6: friend, let us go; let us see the Teacher.”
dhpak1.9:45.1: Now it was a distinguishing trait of the Elder Sāriputta that he always held a teacher in profound respect.
dhpak1.9:45.2: Therefore he said to his friend: “Friend, let us inform our teacher, the wanderer Sañjaya, that we have attained the Deathless.
dhpak1.9:45.3: {1.94} Thus will his mind be awakened, and he will comprehend. But should he fail to [28.202] comprehend, he will at any
dhpak1.9:45.4: rate believe what we say to be true; and so soon as he has listened to the teaching of the Buddhas, he will attain the
dhpak1.9:45.5: paths and the fruitions.” Accordingly the two wanderers went to Sañjaya.
dhpak1.9:46.1: When Sañjaya saw them, he asked: “Friends, did you succeed in finding anyone able to show you the way to the Deathless?”
dhpak1.9:46.2: – “Yes, teacher, such a one have we found. The Buddha has appeared in the world, the Dhamma has appeared, the Saṅgha has appeared.
dhpak1.9:46.3: You, sir, are wandering empty, without the essence. Come, sir, let us go to the Teacher.” – “You may go; I cannot go.”
dhpak1.9:46.4: – “For what reason?” – “In the past I have gone about as a teacher of the multitude. For me to live the life of a pupil
dhpak1.9:46.5: would be like a pot becoming a ladle. I shall not be able to live the life of a pupil.”
dhpak1.9:47.1: “Do not act thus, teacher.” – “Never mind, friends, you may go, but I cannot go.” – “Teacher, from the moment of the
dhpak1.9:47.2: Buddha’s appearance in the world the populace will take perfumes, garlands, and so forth in their hands and will go and
dhpak1.9:47.3: do honor to him alone. Let us also go there. What do you intend to do?” – “Friends, which are more numerous in this world,
dhpak1.9:47.4: the stupid or the wise?” – “Teacher, the stupid are many, the wise are few.” – “Well then, friends, let the wise men go
dhpak1.9:47.5: to the wise ascetic Gotama, and let the stupid come to stupid me. {1.95} You may go, but I shall not go.”
dhpak1.9:47.6: – “You will become a famous man, teacher!” said his two former pupils, and departed. As they departed, Sañjaya’s assembly broke up;
dhpak1.9:47.7: at that instant the grove was empty. When Sañjaya saw that the grove was empty, he vomited hot blood.
dhpak1.9:47.8: Five hundred wanderers accompanied the two on their journey a little way. Of these, two hundred and fifty remained loyal
dhpak1.9:47.9: to Sañjaya and turned back; the other two hundred and fifty wanderers the two received as their own pupils and took with them to Veḷuvana.
dhpak1.9:48.1: As the Teacher sat in the midst of the fourfold assembly teaching the Dhamma, he saw the two wanderers approaching from afar.
dhpak1.9:48.2: Straightaway he addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, here come two friends, Kolita and Upatissa. They will become my pair of disciples,
dhpak1.9:48.3: my chief and noble pair.” The two wanderers worshipped the Teacher, sat down respectfully on one side, and spoke thus to the Teacher:
dhpak1.9:48.4: “Venerable Sir, we should like to receive the going forth at the hands of the Fortunate One; we should like to take higher ordination.”
dhpak1.9:48.5: Said the Fortunate One: “Come, bhikkhus! The Dhamma has been well taught. Lead the holy life, to the end that all suffering
dhpak1.9:48.6: may be utterly done away.” Instantly they became possessed of [28.203] bowls and robes created by supernatural power,
dhpak1.9:48.7: and became, as it were, elders of a hundred years’ seniority.
dhpak1.9:49.1: By the acts of the company of his disciples the Teacher caused the teaching of the Dhamma constantly to increase.
dhpak1.9:49.2: With the exception of the two Chief Disciples all attained Arahatship. The two Chief Disciples, however, did not complete
dhpak1.9:49.3: the meditations leading to the three higher paths. What was the reason for this? It was because of the magnitude of the
dhpak1.9:49.4: perfection of knowledge of Chief Disciples.
dhpak1.9:50.1: Now venerable Mahā Moggallāna, {1.96} residing near the village Kallavāḷa in the kingdom of Magadha, fell into sloth and
dhpak1.9:50.2: torpor on the seventh day after the day of his going forth. But aroused by the Teacher, he shook off sloth and torpor,
dhpak1.9:50.3: and applying himself to the meditation subject on the elements given him by the Realised One, completed the meditations
dhpak1.9:50.4: leading to the three higher paths and attained the goal of the perfection of knowledge of Chief Disciples.
dhpak1.9:51.1: As for the Elder Sāriputta, he spent the fortnight following his going forth with the Teacher, residing at Sūkarakhata
dhpak1.9:51.2: Cave near the same city Rājagaha. Having heard an exposition of the Discourse about Grasping at Feelings to his own sister’s son,
dhpak1.9:51.3: the wandering bhikkhu Dīghanakha, he applied his mind to the Discourse, and like a man who eats rice boiled for another man,
dhpak1.9:51.4: attained the goal of the perfection of knowledge of Chief Disciples.
dhpak1.9:52.1: Surely the Venerable Sāriputta is a man of great intelligence. Why, then, does he require a longer time than Mahā Moggallāna
dhpak1.9:52.2: to attain the goal of the perfection of knowledge of Chief Disciples? Because the preliminaries are so elaborate.
dhpak1.9:52.3: We must understand that the case is analogous to that of a king, who, when he wishes to set out on a journey,
dhpak1.9:52.4: is obliged to make great preparations, such as caparisoning riding-elephants. On the other hand a poor man,
dhpak1.9:52.5: no matter where he may wish to go, immediately goes there without more ado.
dhpak1.9:53.1: On the very day when Sāriputta and Moggallāna were given the going forth, as the shadows of evening lengthened,
dhpak1.9:53.2: the Teacher gathered his disciples together at Veḷuvana, assigned the place of Chief Disciples to the newcomers,
dhpak1.9:53.3: and then recited the Pātimokkha. The bhikkhus were offended and said: “The Teacher shows favoritism in bestowing this distinction.
dhpak1.9:53.4: In bestowing the place of Chief Disciples, he ought to give the preference to those who were the first to go forth;
dhpak1.9:53.5: namely, the Group of Five. If he disregard their claims, he ought to give the preference to the Elder Yasa and his [28.204]
dhpak1.9:53.6: fifty-four companions. If he disregard their claims, {1.97} he ought to give the preference to the Fortunate Group of Thirty.
dhpak1.9:53.7: If he disregard their claims, he ought to give the preference to the three brothers, Uruvelā Kassapa, Nadī Kassapa,
dhpak1.9:53.8: and Gayā Kassapa. In rejecting the prior claims of all these bhikkhus and giving the place of Chief Disciples to those
dhpak1.9:53.9: who went forth last of all, the Teacher shows favoritism.”
dhpak1.9:54.1: The Teacher asked them: “Bhikkhus, what is the subject you are discussing?” When they told him, he said: “Bhikkhus,
dhpak1.9:54.2: I show no favoritism in bestowing this distinction. On the contrary I bestow on these bhikkhus and on all others that for
dhpak1.9:54.3: which each has made his aspiration. For Aññā Koṇḍañña gave the first fruits of a certain crop nine times,
dhpak1.9:54.4: but in so doing did not make an aspiration for the place of Chief Disciple. On the contrary, in bestowing his gift,
dhpak1.9:54.5: he made the aspiration that he might be the first to win the foremost estate of all; namely, Arahatship.” – “When was that,
dhpak1.9:54.6: venerable Sir?” – “Listen, bhikkhus.” – “Yes, venerable Sir.” Thereupon the Fortunate One related the following
dhpak1.9:55.1: The Unfolding Aspiration 8c Story of the Past: Culla Kāḷa and Mahā Kāḷa
dhpak1.9:56.1: Bhikkhus, 91 aeons of time in the past the Fortunate Vipassī appeared in the world. At that time two brothers,
dhpak1.9:56.2: Mahā Kāḷa and Culla Kāḷa, both of them householders, caused a great field to be planted with rice.
dhpak1.9:56.3: One day Culla Kāḷa went to the rice-field, hulled a kernel of rice, and ate it, and found it unusually sweet.
dhpak1.9:56.4: Shortly afterwards he desired to make a gift of unripe rice to the assembly of bhikkhus presided over by the Buddha.
dhpak1.9:56.5: So he went to his older brother and said to him: “Friend, let us have unripe rice hulled and cooked in a manner suitable
dhpak1.9:56.6: for the Buddhas, and let us bestow the same in alms.” – “What say you, brother? No one has ever yet had unripe rice hulled
dhpak1.9:56.7: and given in alms, nor is anyone likely to do such a thing in the future; don’t spoil the crop.”
dhpak1.9:57.1: The younger brother repeated his suggestion several times. {1.98} Finally the older brother said: “Very well,
dhpak1.9:57.2: divide the field into two parts. Do not touch my portion, but do whatever you like in your own portion of the field.”
dhpak1.9:57.3: – “Very well,” said Culla Kāḷa. So he divided the field into two parts, hired a large number of men for manual labor,
dhpak1.9:57.4: caused grains of unripe rice to be hulled, had it cooked in rich milk, adding ghee, honey, and sugar, and presented the
dhpak1.9:57.5: rice thus prepared to the assembly of bhikkhus presided over by the Buddha, saying [28.205] at the conclusion of the meal:
dhpak1.9:57.6: “Venerable Sir, by virtue of this my gift of first-fruits may I be the first to win the foremost estate of all; namely,
dhpak1.9:57.7: Arahatship.” – “So be it,” said the Teacher, returning thanks.
dhpak1.9:58.1: When he went back to the field and looked at it again, he saw that the entire field was filled with heads of growing rice,
dhpak1.9:58.2: bound together, as it were, in sheaves. At this sight he experienced the five kinds of joy. He thought: “I am indeed fortunate.”
dhpak1.9:58.3: When the rice was in the ear, he gave first-fruits of rice in the ear. In association with the residents of the village
dhpak1.9:58.4: he bestowed the first-fruits of the crop. When the rice was reaped, he gave the first-fruits of the reaping;
dhpak1.9:58.5: when it was in the sheaf, the first-fruits of the sheaves; when it was in a pile, the first-fruits of the pile;
dhpak1.9:58.6: when it was in the stack, the first-fruits of the stack; when it was threshed, the first-fruits of the threshing-floor;
dhpak1.9:58.7: when it was ground, the first-fruits of the flour; when it was measured, the first-fruits of the measuring;
dhpak1.9:58.8: when it was put away in the storehouse, the first-fruits of the store. Thus he bestowed the first-fruits of single crop nine times.
dhpak1.9:58.9: Whatever he took away was made up, and he had a bumper harvest. Goodness keeps him who keeps it.
dhpak1.9:60.1: The Dhamma protects one living by it, The Dhamma well-practised brings happiness, This is the advantage of the Dhamma:
dhpak1.9:60.2: It does not lead to bad destinations.
dhpak1.9:61.1: Thus, in the dispensation of the Sambuddha Vipassī, Aññā Koṇḍañña bestowed the gift of first fruits nine times,
dhpak1.9:61.2: making the aspiration to be the first to attain the foremost of all estates. Likewise in the dispensation of the Buddha Padumuttara,
dhpak1.9:61.3: 100,000 aeons of time in the past, in the city of Haṁsavatī, he gave mighty gifts, and falling at the feet of that Fortunate Buddha,
dhpak1.9:61.4: made the aspiration to be the first to attain the foremost of all estates; namely, Arahatship. Thus I bestowed on him only
dhpak1.9:61.5: that for which he made his aspiration. I show no favoritism in bestowing distinction.”
dhpak1.9:62.1: The Aspiration “Venerable Sir, what work of merit did the fifty-five noble youths led by Yasa perform?”
dhpak1.9:62.2: – “They too made an aspiration for Arahatship at the feet of a certain Buddha and did many works of merit.
dhpak1.9:63.1: 8d Story of the Past: Yasa and his Fifty-Four Companions
dhpak1.9:64.1: Afterwards, when a Buddha had appeared in the world, they became friends, banded themselves together for [28.206] the
dhpak1.9:64.2: performance of works of merit, and devoted themselves to the care of the corpses of paupers. One day, seeing the dead body
dhpak1.9:64.3: of a pregnant woman, they carried the body to the cemetery for the purpose of burning it. To Yasa and four of his companions
dhpak1.9:64.4: was assigned the duty of burning the corpse; the rest returned and entered the village.
dhpak1.9:65.1: As the youth Yasa burned the body, piercing it with stakes and turning it over and over, he grasped the thought of the impurity of the body.
dhpak1.9:65.2: This thought he communicated to his four companions also, saying: “Behold, friends, this body. Here and there the skin has burst open;
dhpak1.9:65.3: it resembles nothing so much as the skin of a mottled cow. It is impure, stinking, {1.100} repulsive.”
dhpak1.9:66.1: Straightaway his four companions also grasped the thought of the impurity of the body. In their turn these five companions
dhpak1.9:66.2: went to the village and informed the rest of their friends. As for Yasa, he went home and informed his mother and father and wife,
dhpak1.9:66.3: and they all developed the thought of impurity.
dhpak1.9:67.1: This is their previous deed. And because of this very work of merit, consciousness of the impurity of the body arose within
dhpak1.9:67.2: Yasa’s mind in the women’s apartments. And thus, because they had acquired the supporting conditions thereto,
dhpak1.9:67.3: all of them developed specific attainment. Therefore these youths also obtained precisely that for which they made their aspiration.
dhpak1.9:67.4: I show no favoritism in bestowing distinction.”
dhpak1.9:68.1: “But, venerable Sir, what work of merit did the Fortunate Group of thirty perform?” – “They also made an aspiration for
dhpak1.9:68.2: Arahatship at the feet of previous Buddhas and performed works of merit.
dhpak1.9:70.1: Afterwards, when a Buddha had appeared in the world, they were reborn as thirty wrongdoers; but hearing the admonition
dhpak1.9:70.2: addressed to Tuṇḍila, they kept the five precepts for sixty thousand years.
dhpak1.9:71.1: Thus these men also obtained only that for which they made their aspiration. I show no favoritism in bestowing distinction.”
dhpak1.9:72.1: “But, venerable Sir, what work of merit was performed by tUruvelā Kassapa and so on?” – “They also performed works of merit,
dhpak1.9:72.2: making an aspiration to attain Arahatship.
dhpak1.9:73.1: 8f Story of the Past: Three Brothers Kassapa
dhpak1.9:74.1: Ninety-two aeons of time in the past, two [28.207] Buddhas appeared in the world in the same aeon, Tissa and Phussa;
dhpak1.9:74.2: Phussa’s father was King Mahinda. When Phussa attained Awakening, the king’s youngest son became his Chief Disciple,
dhpak1.9:74.3: and the son of the Brahmin chaplain became his Second Disciple. The king went to the Teacher and said:
dhpak1.9:74.4: ‘My oldest son is the Buddha, my youngest son is Chief Disciple, and the son of my Brahmin chaplain is Second Disciple.’
dhpak1.9:74.5: And looking upon the three, he said: ‘My very own is the Buddha, my very own is the Dhamma, my very own is the Saṅgha.’
dhpak1.9:74.6: And thrice he breathed forth the exalted utterance: ‘Reverence to him, the Fortunate One, the Arahat, the Perfect Sambuddha.’
dhpak1.9:74.7: Then he prostrated himself before the feet of the Teacher and said: {1.101} ‘Venerable Sir, now, at the end of a life
dhpak1.9:74.8: lasting ninety thousand years, it is time, as it were, for me to sit down and close my eyes in slumber. So long as I live,
dhpak1.9:74.9: go not to the door of others’ houses, but receive the four requisites from me alone.’ Having thus obtained the Teacher’s consent,
dhpak1.9:74.10: the king thereafter attended on him regularly.
dhpak1.9:75.1: Now the king had three other sons besides, the eldest of whom had a retinue of five hundred soldiers, the middlemost three,
dhpak1.9:75.2: and the youngest two. One day they sought permission of their father to entertain their brother, the Buddha Phussa,
dhpak1.9:75.3: but failed to obtain it. This happened many times.
dhpak1.9:76.1: Shortly afterwards an insurrection broke out on the frontier, and they were sent to suppress it. Succeeding in restoring
dhpak1.9:76.2: order on the frontier, they returned to their father. Their father embraced them, kissed their heads, and said to them:
dhpak1.9:76.3: ‘Dear sons, I grant you whatever you desire.’ – ‘Very well, your majesty,’ said they, accepting his offer.
dhpak1.9:76.4: When, after a few days, their father again said: ‘Dear sons, I grant you whatever you desire,’ they replied: ‘Your majesty,
dhpak1.9:76.5: we desire nothing else but only this, that henceforth we may entertain our brother; grant us this boon.’
dhpak1.9:76.6: – ‘I will not grant you this boon, dear sons.’ – ‘If you are unwilling to grant us this privilege permanently,
dhpak1.9:76.7: then grant it to us for seven years.’ – ‘That I will not, dear sons.’ – ‘Well then, grant us the privilege for six years,
dhpak1.9:76.8: or five, or four, or three, or two years, or for one year; or for seven months, or six, or five, or four, or three months.’
dhpak1.9:76.9: – ‘That I will not, dear sons.’ – ‘Well then, your majesty, make it one month for each of us; grant us this privilege for
dhpak1.9:76.10: three months in all.’ – ‘Very well, dear sons; then entertain your brother for three months.’
dhpak1.9:77.1: Now all three brothers had a single rich man and a single steward, the latter of whom had a retinue of 120,000 serving-men.
dhpak1.9:77.2: [28.208] The three brothers summoned the rich man and the steward {1.102} and said to them: ‘During the coming three months
dhpak1.9:77.3: we shall take upon ourselves the ten precepts, put on the yellow robes, and reside with the Teacher.
dhpak1.9:77.4: In our absence it will be your duty to administer the alms; every day you are to provide all the food, both hard and soft,
dhpak1.9:77.5: for ninety thousand bhikkhus and a thousand soldiers. From henceforth we shall have nothing at all to say.’
dhpak1.9:77.6: So the three brothers took their retinue of a thousand men, took upon themselves the ten precepts, put on the yellow robes,
dhpak1.9:77.7: and began residence in the monastery.
dhpak1.9:78.1: The rich man and the steward joined forces and performed the duty of almsgiving by turns, taking provisions from the
dhpak1.9:78.2: storehouses of the three brothers and bestowing them in alms. But when the children of the serving-men cried for rice-porridge
dhpak1.9:78.3: and other kinds of food, the rich man and the steward would give them what they cried for, even before the assembly of bhikkhus arrived.
dhpak1.9:78.4: The result was that the assembly of bhikkhus received only what was left over at the end of a meal, and not a fresh supply of food at all.
dhpak1.9:78.5: Finally the rich man and the steward became so greedy that they would take food, and pretending that they were going to
dhpak1.9:78.6: give it to the children, eat it themselves. At the mere sight of the pleasing food they were unable to resist.
dhpak1.9:78.7: They and their associates numbered 84,000 men. Because they ate food which it was their duty to give to the assembly of bhikkhus,
dhpak1.9:78.8: when they died and their bodies were dissolved, they were reborn in the Peta Realm.
dhpak1.9:79.1: When the three brothers and their thousand men died, they were reborn in the Deva Realm and spent ninety-two aeons of time
dhpak1.9:79.2: in passing between the Deva Realms to the world of humans.
dhpak1.9:80.1: Thus did those three brothers perform works of merit at that time, making the aspiration to attain Arahatship.
dhpak1.9:80.2: What they received was only that for which they made their aspiration. I show no favoritism in giving what I give.
dhpak1.9:80.3: Now at that time {1.103} their steward was Bimbisāra, their rich man was the lay disciple Visākha, and the three royal
dhpak1.9:80.4: princes were the three ascetics of the matted locks.
dhpak1.9:81.1: Their serving-men, reborn at that time among the Petas, after passing from one state of existence to another, both good and bad,
dhpak1.9:81.2: were reborn in this present world-cycle in the world of the Petas for the space of four Buddha-intervals.
dhpak1.9:81.3: In this present world-cycle they approached first of all the Fortunate Kakusandha, whose term of life was forty thousand years,
dhpak1.9:81.4: and asked him: ‘Tell us when we shall obtain something to eat.’ He replied: ‘You will receive nothing to [28.209] eat in my time;
dhpak1.9:81.5: but after me the great earth will be elevated a league, and the Buddha Koṇāgamana will appear; you had best ask him.’
dhpak1.9:81.6: They waited all that time, and when the Buddha Koṇāgamana appeared, asked him. He replied: ‘You will receive nothing to eat in my time;
dhpak1.9:81.7: but after me the great earth will be elevated a league, and the Buddha Kassapa will appear; you had best ask him.’
dhpak1.9:81.8: They waited all that time, and when the Buddha Kassapa appeared, asked him. He replied: ‘You will receive nothing to eat in my time;
dhpak1.9:81.9: but after me the great earth will be elevated a league, and the Buddha Gotama will appear. At that time your kinsman Bimbisāra will be king;
dhpak1.9:81.10: he will give alms to the Teacher and will make over to you the merit acquired by that act; at that time you will receive something to eat.”
dhpak1.9:82.1: The length of the period intervening between two Buddhas was to them as the morrow. When the Realised One appeared in the
dhpak1.9:82.2: world and King Bimbisāra gave alms on the first day and they failed to receive the fruit thereof, they waited until it was night,
dhpak1.9:82.3: and then made a fearful noise and showed themselves to the king. When the king went to Veḷuvana on the following day,
dhpak1.9:82.4: {1.104} he related the incident to the Realised One. The Teacher said: “Great king, ninety-two aeons of time in the past,
dhpak1.9:82.5: in the dispensation of the Buddha Phussa, these Petas were kinsmen of yours. They ate food which it was their duty to give
dhpak1.9:82.6: to the assembly of bhikkhus, and because of this were reborn in the Peta Realm. Passing through the round of existences,
dhpak1.9:82.7: they asked the Buddhas Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa when they should obtain food, and the Buddhas told them this and that.
dhpak1.9:82.8: All this time they desired greatly to receive your alms; and the reason why they acted as they did last night was that,
dhpak1.9:82.9: when you gave alms, they failed to receive the fruit thereof.” – “But, venerable Sir, in case I were to give alms now,
dhpak1.9:82.10: would they receive the fruit thereof?” – “Yes, great king.”
dhpak1.9:83.1: On the following day the king invited the assembly
dhpak1.9:83.2: of bhikkhus presided over by the Buddha, bestowed abundant offerings,
dhpak1.9:83.3: and said: “Venerable Sir, henceforth may celestial food and drink
dhpak1.9:83.4: be the portion of these Petas.” And when he had thus
dhpak1.9:83.5: transferred to the Petas the merit of his offering, they received celestial food and drink.
dhpak1.9:84.1: On the following day the Petas made their appearance naked. The king said to the Buddha: “To-day, venerable Sir,
dhpak1.9:84.2: these Petas made their appearance naked,” and asked him what he should do. The Teacher said: “Great king, you did not give them clothes.”
dhpak1.9:84.3: So on the following day the king presented robes to the assembly of bhikkhus [28.210] presided over by the Buddha, saying:
dhpak1.9:84.4: “Henceforth may they possess celestial raiment.” And when he had thus made over to them the merit of his offering,
dhpak1.9:84.5: instantly they became possessed of celestial raiment, whereupon they put off their Peta forms and took on the forms of celestial beings.
dhpak1.9:85.1: When the Teacher returned thanks, he said: “They stand beyond the walls,” reciting the Beyond the Walls formula:
dhpak1.9:86.1: They stand beyond the walls, and at the junctions and crossroads, they stand before the door-posts, after coming to their homes.
dhpak1.9:87.1: When abundant food and drink, staple, non-staple, is prepared, nobody remembers them, because of these beings’ deeds.
dhpak1.9:88.1: Thus they give to relatives, those who are compassionate, pure, excellent, and timely, appropriate drinks and food.
dhpak1.9:89.1: “May this go to our relatives, may our relatives be happy!” Those who have come together, the departed relatives,
dhpak1.9:90.1: around the food and the drink, respectfully offer thanks: “May our relatives live long! Those to whom we owe this gain,
dhpak1.9:91.1: for we’ve been honoured, those who give are not without reward!” For there there is no ploughing, cattle-rearing is not found,
dhpak1.9:92.1: there is nothing for trading, buying and selling of gold. From there they depend on gifts, the departed who made time.
dhpak1.9:93.1: Just as water rains on the highlands, flows to the lowlands, so too what has been given benefits the departed.
dhpak1.9:94.1: Just as rivers that are full completely fill the ocean, so too what has been given benefits the departed.
dhpak1.9:95.1: “He gave to me, he worked for me, my kin, friend, companion,” he should give to the departed, remembering what they did.
dhpak1.9:96.1: For no tears, or grief, or any other lamentations, are of use to the departed, just so their relatives remain.
dhpak1.9:97.1: But that gift that has been given, that is well placed in the Sangha, benefits them for a long time, right there it is of benefit.
dhpak1.9:98.1: A relative’s duties has been explained - great honour is done to the departed, strength has also been given to the monks,
dhpak1.9:98.2: no little merit is produced by you!
dhpak1.9:99.1: At the conclusion of his words of thanksgiving 84,000 living beings had comprehension of the Dhamma.
dhpak1.9:99.2: Thus did the Teacher expound the Dhamma, relating the story of the three brothers of the matted locks.
dhpak1.9:100.1: “But, venerable Sir, what work of merit did the Chief Disciples perform?” – “They made their aspiration to attain the
dhpak1.9:100.2: station of Chief Disciples one immeasurable period of time and 100,000 aeons of time additional in the past.
dhpak1.9:101.1: 8g Story of the Past: Sarada and Sirivaḍḍha
dhpak1.9:102.1: Sāriputta was reborn in the family of a Brahmin of great wealth, and was called the young Brahmin Sarada.
dhpak1.9:102.2: Moggallāna {1.105} was reborn in the family of a householder of great wealth, and was called householder Sirivaḍḍha.
dhpak1.9:102.3: The two youths were friends from the time when they played in the dirt together.
dhpak1.9:103.1: The young Brahmin Sarada came into a large family inheritance on the death of his father. One day, when he was alone by himself,
dhpak1.9:103.2: he thought: ‘I have certain knowledge of the life of this world only; I know nothing of the life of the world beyond.
dhpak1.9:103.3: All they that are born are certain to die. I ought to go forth, enter some Saṅgha, and seek the way of release.’
dhpak1.9:103.4: Therefore he approached his friend and said: ‘Friend Sirivaḍḍha, it is my intention to go forth and seek the way of release.
dhpak1.9:103.5: Can you, or can you not, go forth with me?’ – ‘Friend, I cannot go forth; you alone go forth.’ The young Brahmin Sarada thought to himself:
dhpak1.9:103.6: ‘No one ever yet went to the world beyond with companions or kinsmen or friends. What one does, he must do by himself.’
dhpak1.9:104.1: Ascetic and Householder Accordingly he threw open the doors of his treasure-house and bestowed abundant alms on paupers
dhpak1.9:104.2: and travelers and beggars. Having so done, he went forth to the foot of a certain mountain and went forth in the seers’ going forth.
dhpak1.9:104.3: First one, then two, then three, then many others followed his example in adopting the monastic life.
dhpak1.9:104.4: Finally there were 74,000 ascetics with matted locks. Sarada [28.211] acquired the five super knowledges and the eight
dhpak1.9:104.5: higher attainments, and taught those ascetics of the matted locks the processes necessary to the practice of absorption.
dhpak1.9:104.6: All of them acquired the five super knowledges and the eight attainments.
dhpak1.9:105.1: At this time the Buddha Anomadassī appeared in the world. His city was Candavatī. His father was Yasavanta, of the noble caste,
dhpak1.9:105.2: and his mother was Devī Yasodharā. His Bodhi tree was the Ajjuna tree. Nisabha and Anoma were his Chief Disciples,
dhpak1.9:105.3: Varuṇa was his supporter, and Sundarā and Sumanā were his principal female lay disciples. His term of life was 100,000 years,
dhpak1.9:105.4: his stature {1.106} was fifty-eight cubits, and the radiance from his body flashed twelve leagues. He had a retinue of 100,000 bhikkhus.
dhpak1.9:106.1: One day at dawn, arising from a meditation of great compassion, he surveyed the world and beheld the ascetic Sarada.
dhpak1.9:106.2: Thereupon he became aware of the following: ‘To-day, through my approaching the ascetic Sarada, there will be a mighty
dhpak1.9:106.3: teaching of the Dhamma. Sarada will make his aspiration for the place of Chief Disciple, and his friend, the householder Sirivaḍḍha,
dhpak1.9:106.4: will make his aspiration for the place of Second Disciple. At the conclusion of the discourse the 74,000 ascetics with
dhpak1.9:106.5: matted locks who compose his retinue will attain Arahatship. Therefore it is necessary for me to go there.’
dhpak1.9:107.1: Accordingly, taking his own bowl and robe, saying not a word to anyone else, proceeding in solitude like a lion, he commanded:
dhpak1.9:107.2: ‘Let Sarada know that I am the Buddha.’ And while the ascetic Sarada’s pupils were absent seeking various kinds of fruits,
dhpak1.9:107.3: he descended from the sky and alighted on the earth before Sarada’s very eyes.
dhpak1.9:108.1: When the ascetic Sarada beheld the supernatural power of the Buddha and the perfection of form of the Buddha,
dhpak1.9:108.2: he pondered in his mind the mantras relating to the characteristics of a great man. And he said to himself:
dhpak1.9:108.3: ‘One endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, is a king, a Universal Monarch. Having gone forth,
dhpak1.9:108.4: he is one who has rolled back the veil of passion, an Omniscient Buddha. This man is without doubt a Buddha.’
dhpak1.9:109.1: Therefore he advanced to meet him, worshipped him with the five limbs, prepared a seat and offered it to him.
dhpak1.9:109.2: The Fortunate One seated himself in the seat prepared for him, and the ascetic Sarada, selecting a seat appropriate to himself,
dhpak1.9:109.3: sat down respectfully on one side.
dhpak1.9:110.1: At that moment the 74,000 ascetics of the matted locks, who had been absent gathering various kinds of sweet and juicy fruits,
dhpak1.9:110.2: returned to their teacher. Seeing the Buddha seated and their [28.212] own teacher seated near him, they said:
dhpak1.9:110.3: {1.107} ‘Teacher, we used to go about this world thinking to ourselves: “There is no one greater than you.”
dhpak1.9:110.4: But as for this man, we are certain that he is greater than you.’ – ‘Friends, what say you? Do you mean to compare a grain
dhpak1.9:110.5: of mustard seed to Mount Sineru, 68,000 leagues high? Little sons, do not compare me to an Omniscient Buddha.’
dhpak1.9:110.6: Then those ascetics thought to themselves: ‘Were this an insignificant man, our teacher would not use such a comparison as this.
dhpak1.9:110.7: How great indeed must this man be!’ And forthwith they fell before his feet and prostrated themselves before him.
dhpak1.9:111.1: Then their teacher said to them: ‘Friends, we have here no offering suitable to present to the Buddhas, and the Teacher
dhpak1.9:111.2: has come here at a time when we usually go the rounds for alms; let us give him gifts according to our ability.
dhpak1.9:111.3: Fetch here all manner of fruits that are choicest.’ And having thus caused them to fetch fruits, he washed his hands and
dhpak1.9:111.4: himself placed the fruits in the bowl of the Realised One. The moment the Teacher touched the fruits which were brought,
dhpak1.9:111.5: the Devatās imparted a celestial flavor to them. The ascetic Sarada also himself filtered water and presented it to the Teacher.
dhpak1.9:111.6: After the meal was over, while the Teacher still remained seated, Sarada summoned all of his pupils, and sitting down,
dhpak1.9:112.1: The Teacher thought to himself: ‘Let the two Chief Disciples approach, together with the assembly of bhikkhus.’
dhpak1.9:112.2: Straightaway together with their retinue of 100,000 Arahats they approached, worshipped the Teacher, and sat down respectfully on one side.
dhpak1.9:112.3: Then the ascetic Sarada {1.108} addressed his pupils as follows: ‘Friends, the seat wherein sit the Buddhas is low,
dhpak1.9:112.4: and there is no seat for the 100,000 bhikkhus. To-day you should render high honor to the Buddha. Fetch from the foot of
dhpak1.9:112.5: the mountain flowers possessing bright colors and sweet perfumes.’
dhpak1.9:113.1: There is a saying: ‘Time occupied in talk is wasted; inconceivable is the range of psychic power possessed by one endowed
dhpak1.9:113.2: with supernatural power,’ and so it was in this case. In but an instant those ascetics brought back flowers possessing
dhpak1.9:113.3: bright colors and sweet perfumes and arranged a cushion of flowers a league long for the Buddhas. Then they arranged a
dhpak1.9:113.4: cushion of flowers three quarters of a league long for the two Chief Disciples. The cushions for the rest of the bhikkhus
dhpak1.9:113.5: were half a league long or less; those for the novices were 640 metres long. It is not permissible to ask the question:
dhpak1.9:113.6: ‘How could seats of such great [28.213] size be arranged in this hermitage?’ This was made possible by psychic power.
dhpak1.9:113.7: When the seats had thus been made ready, the ascetic Sarada took his stand before the Realised One, and raising his clasped
dhpak1.9:113.8: hands in an attitude of reverent salutation, said: ‘Venerable Sir, ascend this bed of flowers to my everlasting welfare and salvation.’
dhpak1.9:114.1: Having gathered various flowers and scents into one, and prepared a flower seat, this is the word that he spoke:
dhpak1.9:115.1: ‘Sit on this, my prepared seat, Hero, if it is suitable, bring confidence to my mind on this seat made of flowers.’
dhpak1.9:116.1: The Buddha, for seven nights and days sat on the flower seat, bringing confidence, gladdening my mind, (in the world) together with its Devas.
dhpak1.9:117.1: While the Teacher sat thus, the two Chief Disciples with the rest of the bhikkhus {1.109} sat each in the seat which had
dhpak1.9:117.2: been prepared for him. The ascetic Sarada, taking a great flower-parasol, held it over the head of the Realised One.
dhpak1.9:117.3: The Teacher said: ‘May this honor rendered to me by the ascetics of the matted locks yield rich fruit.’
dhpak1.9:117.4: And straightaway he entered into a state of absorption, attaining cessation. Observing that the Teacher had attained cessation,
dhpak1.9:117.5: the two Chief Disciples likewise entered into a state of absorption and attained cessation.
dhpak1.9:118.1: For seven days the Teacher sat there, enjoying the bliss of cessation. When it was time to seek food, Sarada’s pupils went
dhpak1.9:118.2: into the forest and ate wild fruits and other varieties of fruits. The rest of the time they stood holding out their hands
dhpak1.9:118.3: in an attitude of reverent salutation before the Buddhas. The ascetic Sarada, however, went not to seek food,
dhpak1.9:118.4: but for seven days continuously held the flower-parasol over the Buddha, experiencing thereby intense joy and pleasure.
dhpak1.9:119.1: When the Teacher arose from absorption, he said to his Chief Disciple the Elder Nisabha, who sat on his right hand:
dhpak1.9:119.2: ‘Nisabha, return thanks to the ascetics who have honored us with flowers and seats.’ Thereupon the elder,
dhpak1.9:119.3: like a mighty warrior who has just received high distinction at the hands of a Universal Monarch, his heart filled with joy,
dhpak1.9:119.4: manifesting the perfection of knowledge capable of attainment by a disciple, began the address of thanksgiving for the flowers and seats.
dhpak1.9:119.5: At the end of the discourse the Buddha addressed the Second Disciple as follows: ‘Do you also teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus.’
dhpak1.9:119.6: Thereupon the Elder Anoma, pondering the Three Baskets, the word of [28.214] the Buddhas, taught the Dhamma.
dhpak1.9:119.7: But although the two Chief Disciples taught the Dhamma, no single bhikkhu present attained comprehension of the Dhamma.
dhpak1.9:120.1: Then the Teacher, manifesting the infinite power of a Buddha, began to teach the Dhamma, with the result that at the
dhpak1.9:120.2: conclusion of his discourse all 74,000 ascetics of the matted locks attained Arahatship, with the sole exception of the ascetic Sarada.
dhpak1.9:120.3: Then the Teacher stretched forth his hand and said to them: ‘Come, bhikkhus!’ Instantly their hair and beard disappeared,
dhpak1.9:120.4: and the eight requisites were attached to their persons.
dhpak1.9:121.1: Do you ask: ‘Why did not the ascetic Sarada attain Arahatship?’ It was because his mind was distracted.
dhpak1.9:121.2: We are told that when he seated himself in the seat of the Second Disciple of the Buddhas, {1.110} and the Chief Disciple,
dhpak1.9:121.3: manifesting the perfection of knowledge of a disciple, taught the Dhamma, at the very moment when he began to listen to
dhpak1.9:121.4: the teaching of the Dhamma by the Chief Disciple, the following thought arose in his mind: ‘Oh that at some time in the future,
dhpak1.9:121.5: in the dispensation of a Buddha who shall arise hereafter, I might receive the burden which this disciple has received!
dhpak1.9:121.6: Because of this thought, we are told, he was unable to attain the paths and the fruitions.
dhpak1.9:122.1: Sarada, however, worshipped the Realised One, and standing face to face with him, said: ‘Venerable Sir, what is the title
dhpak1.9:122.2: in your dispensation borne by the bhikkhu who sits in the seat next to you?’ – ‘He it is that follows me in setting in
dhpak1.9:122.3: motion the Wheel of the Dhamma which I have set in motion; he it is that has reached the pinnacle of the perfection of
dhpak1.9:122.4: knowledge capable of attainment by a disciple; he it is that has grasped the sixteen forms of knowledge;
dhpak1.9:122.5: he it is that is therefore called in my dispensation a Chief Disciple.’ – ‘Venerable Sir, here for seven days have I stood
dhpak1.9:122.6: holding the flower-parasol over you, thereby rendering honor to you. As the fruit of this work of merit,
dhpak1.9:122.7: I do not wish for a second existence as Sakka or Brahma. But at some time in the future may I become the Chief Disciple
dhpak1.9:122.8: of a certain Buddha, even as is this present Elder Nisabha.’
dhpak1.9:123.1: When Sarada had made this aspiration, the Teacher considered within himself: ‘Will the aspiration of this man be fulfilled?’
dhpak1.9:123.2: Therefore he sent forth his perception into the future, and surveying the ages of the future, he passed before his mind
dhpak1.9:123.3: a period of incalculable length and 100,000 aeons of time in addition; whereupon he saw that his aspiration would be fulfilled.
dhpak1.9:123.4: So when the Teacher saw that his aspiration would be fulfilled, he said to the ascetic Sarada: ‘This aspiration of yours
dhpak1.9:123.5: will not be in vain. For at the end of a period of incalculable [28.215] length and 100,000 aeons of time in addition,
dhpak1.9:123.6: Gotama Buddha will appear in the world. His mother will be Queen Mahā Māyā, his father will be King Suddhodana,
dhpak1.9:123.7: his son will be Rāhula, his attendant will be Ānanda, and his Second Disciple will be Moggallāna. And you will be his Chief Disciple,
dhpak1.9:123.8: the Captain of the Dhamma, and your name will be Sāriputta.’
dhpak1.9:124.1: The Aspiration When the Teacher had thus predicted the future of the ascetic, he taught the Dhamma, and then,
dhpak1.9:124.2: surrounded by his company of bhikkhus, flew up into the air and departed. The ascetic Sarada sought out the pupils and
dhpak1.9:124.3: elders and sent the following message to his friend, the householder Sirivaḍḍha: ‘Venerable Sirs, say to my friend:
dhpak1.9:124.4: “Your friend the ascetic Sarada fell down before the feet of the Buddha Anomadassī and made his aspiration for the place
dhpak1.9:124.5: of Chief Disciple under the dispensation of the Buddha Gotama, who shall hereafter arise in the world.
dhpak1.9:124.6: Do you make your aspiration for the place of Second Disciple.”’ And when he had thus spoken, he preceded the elders by a
dhpak1.9:124.7: different route and went and stood at the door of Sirivaḍḍha’s residence.
dhpak1.9:125.1: When Sirivaḍḍha saw him he said: ‘At last, after a long absence, my noble friend has returned.’ And straightaway he seated
dhpak1.9:125.2: his friend in a seat, and having seated himself in a lower seat, asked him: ‘But, venerable Sir, have you no pupils and attendants?’
dhpak1.9:125.3: – ‘Yes, my friend, the Buddha Anomadassī came to our hermitage, and we did him honor to the extent of our power.
dhpak1.9:125.4: The Teacher taught the Dhamma to all, and at the conclusion of his discourse all the members of our community excepting
dhpak1.9:125.5: me attained Arahatship and went forth. When I saw the Chief Disciple of the Teacher, the Elder Nisabha,
dhpak1.9:125.6: I made my aspiration for the place of Chief Disciple under the dispensation of the Buddha Gotama, who shall hereafter arise in the world.
dhpak1.9:125.7: Do you also make your aspiration for the place of Second Disciple under his dispensation.’ – ‘But, venerable Sir,
dhpak1.9:125.8: I am not on terms of familiar acquaintance with the Buddhas.’ – ‘I will assume the burden of talking with the Buddhas;
dhpak1.9:126.1: When Sirivaḍḍha heard his words, he adorned a space eight acres in extent before the door of his residence with the respect
dhpak1.9:126.2: due to a king, sprinkled sand, {1.112} scattered flowers of five kinds, including Takoli flowers, caused a pavilion to be
dhpak1.9:126.3: erected with a thatch of blue lotuses, caused the seat of the Buddha to be made ready, and seats for the bhikkhus also to be prepared.
dhpak1.9:126.4: And having caused abundant offerings and gifts to be prepared, he directed the ascetic Sarada to [28.216] invite the Buddhas.
dhpak1.9:126.5: So the ascetic took the assembly of bhikkhus presided over by the Buddha and went with them to Sirivaḍḍha’s residence,
dhpak1.9:126.6: advanced to meet them, took the bowl from the hand of the Realised One, conducted them into the pavilion,
dhpak1.9:126.7: seated the assembly of bhikkhus on the seats prepared for them, offered them with the water of donation,
dhpak1.9:126.8: and provided them with the choicest food.
dhpak1.9:127.1: At the conclusion of the meal, having clothed the assembly of bhikkhus with robes of great price, he said to the Teacher:
dhpak1.9:127.2: ‘Venerable Sir, it was for the purpose of gaining no mean place that this entertainment was undertaken.
dhpak1.9:127.3: Show your gracious compassion by remaining here in this manner for a period of seven days.’ The Teacher condescended to remain.
dhpak1.9:127.4: For seven days Sirivaḍḍha bestowed abundant offerings in this manner. At the end of his almsgiving he worshipped the Teacher,
dhpak1.9:127.5: and standing before him with hands clasped in an attitude of reverent salutation, said: ‘Venerable Sir,
dhpak1.9:127.6: my friend the ascetic Sarada made his aspiration to become Chief Disciple of a certain Teacher. May I also become his Second Disciple.’
dhpak1.9:128.1: The Teacher looked into the future, and beholding the fulfillment of his aspiration, made the following prophecy:
dhpak1.9:128.2: ‘At the end of a period of incalculable length and 100,000 aeons of time in addition, you will become the Second Disciple of Gotama Buddha.’
dhpak1.9:128.3: Hearing this prophecy of the Buddhas, Sirivaḍḍha was filled with joy and satisfaction. The Teacher returned thanks for
dhpak1.9:128.4: the offering of food, and then, surrounded by the company of bhikkhus, returned to the monastery.
dhpak1.9:129.1: This, bhikkhus, was the aspiration made by my sons at that time. They have received precisely that for which they made their aspiration.
dhpak1.9:129.2: When I give, I give without respect of persons.
dhpak1.9:130.1: When the Teacher had thus spoken, the two Chief Disciples worshipped the Fortunate One and said: “Venerable Sir,
dhpak1.9:130.2: when we were yet householders, we went to see the festivities of the Mountain-Top,” and then told the entire story of the
dhpak1.9:130.3: events which had recently taken place, to their attainment of Stream-entry at the hands of the Elder Assaji. Then they said:
dhpak1.9:130.4: “Venerable Sir, we went to our teacher, desiring to lead him to your feet, and pointed out to him the shallowness of his own views,
dhpak1.9:130.5: and dwelt upon the advantages of his coming here. But he said to us: ‘For me to live the life of a pupil would be like a
dhpak1.9:130.6: (full) pot becoming an (empty) bucket. I shall not be able to live the life of a pupil.’ We replied: ‘Teacher,
dhpak1.9:130.7: [28.217] the populace will now take perfumes, garlands, and so forth in their hands, and will go to do honor to the Teacher alone.
dhpak1.9:130.8: What do you intend to do?’ He said: ‘Which are the more numerous in this world, the stupid or the wise?’ We replied:
dhpak1.9:130.9: ‘Teacher, the stupid are many; the wise are few.’ – ‘Well then,’ said he: ‘let the wise men go to the wise ascetic Gotama,
dhpak1.9:130.10: and let the stupid come to stupid me. As for you, go where you like.’ With these words, venerable Sir, did he refuse to come here.”
dhpak1.9:131.1: When the Teacher heard this, he said: “Bhikkhus, by reason of the wrong views which he holds, Sañjaya has mistaken falsehood
dhpak1.9:131.2: for truth and truth for falsehood. But you, by reason of your own wisdom, have rightly discerned that which is true in
dhpak1.9:131.3: its truth and that which is false in its falsity, and you have done wisely to reject that which is false and accept that which is true.”
dhpak1.9:131.4: So saying, he pronounced the following verses:
dhpak1.9:132.1: 11. Asāre sāramatino, sāre cāsāradassino, te sāraṁ nādhigacchanti, micchāsaṅkappagocarā.
dhpak1.9:133.1: Finding the essential in the unessential, seeing the unessential in the essential, they do not understand what is the essential,
dhpak1.9:134.1: 12. Sārañ-ca sārato ñatvā, asārañ-ca asārato, te sāraṁ adhigacchanti, sammāsaṅkappagocarā.
dhpak1.9:135.1: Knowing the essential in what is essential, and the unessential in the unessential, they come to understand what is the essential,
dhpak1.9:136.1: At the conclusion of these verses many reached the fruition of Stream-entry, and those who had assembled also had benefit
